papers.title: Influenza A-Associated Encephalitis and Encephalopathy in Adults: An Exploratory Criteria-Based Analysis.
papers.abstract: Influenza A can cause encephalopathy or encephalitis, yet adult data are scarce and the two entities are seldom distinguished systematically. This small retrospective study of five adults explored the feasibility and limitations of classifying these complications with the International Encephalitis Consortium (IEC) 2013 criteria and describes their clinical, radiological, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and treatment characteristics. We retrospectively reviewed five consecutive adults admitted to a tertiary center with polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-confirmed influenza A and acute neurological symptoms, all evaluated with brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), lumbar puncture, and electroencephalography (EEG). Encephalitis was defined by the IEC 2013 criteria (altered mental status > 24 h plus ≥ 2 minor criteria of central nervous system (CNS) inflammation). Data were analyzed descriptively. Three patients met criteria for encephalitis and two for encephalopathy (four women; age 44-68 years). Respiratory influenza A PCR was positive and CSF PCR negative in all. CSF pleocytosis occurred in two patients, bilateral thalamic and subcortical white matter MRI hyperintensities in two, generalized EEG slowing in four, and focal status epilepticus in one. All received oseltamivir; three received high-dose methylprednisolone, two of whom also required intravenous immunoglobulin and plasma exchange. The categories overlapped substantially: EEG slowing and negative CSF PCR occurred in both, and treatment escalation followed clinical course rather than category, with the most intensive regimen required by one patient in each. At 3 months, three patients were asymptomatic and two, both with encephalitis and structural MRI lesions, had persistent deficits. In this small, hypothesis-generating study, IEC-based classification was feasible, but encephalitis and encephalopathy overlapped substantially and the distinction did not determine treatment. The main contribution lies in illustrating both the feasibility and limitations of criteria-based classification in adults with influenza A, rather than in establishing its clinical utility.

papers.title: De novo POLR2A p.(L1127F) variant presenting with neurodevelopmental regression and dystonia, with favorable response to low-dose dopamine therapy: a case report and literature review.
papers.abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia and variable intellectual and behavioral abnormalities (NEDHIB) is a rare autosomal-dominant condition caused by pathogenic POLR2A variants. It typically presents in infancy with hypotonia, developmental delay, and multisystem manifestations. Fewer than 40 patients have been reported worldwide, suggesting frequent misdiagnosis and underdiagnosis. To our knowledge, neurodevelopmental regression has not been documented in confirmed NEDHIB cases, and no standardized therapeutic regimens are established for clinical management. The patient presented with neonatal hypotonia and developmental delay. At 2 years and 4 months, she developed sleep-associated dystonia-like nodding and limb tremors that were initially suspected to represent epileptic seizures. By 3 years of age, she exhibited marked neurodevelopmental regression: loss of the ability to walk and sit independently, together with deterioration of language function. Electroencephalography (EEG) demonstrated background slowing accompanied by epileptiform discharges. Whole-exome sequencing identified a de novo heterozygous POLR2A variant c.3379C > T (p. L1127F), which confirmed the diagnosis of NEDHIB. Long-term rehabilitation training yielded only modest clinical benefits. After initiation of the dopamine agent levodopa-benserazide hydrochloride, marked improvements in motor and cognitive performance were observed, accompanied by the complete resolution of nodding episodes. With dose titration during follow-up, her clinical status remained stable without symptom relapse. This case expands the phenotypic spectrum associated with POLR2A-related NEDHIB and suggests that neurodevelopmental regression may occur within the phenotypic spectrum of this disorder. Our findings also highlight the potential benefit of low-dose dopamine therapy, offering novel insights into the clinical diagnosis, differential diagnosis, and therapeutic management of NEDHIB.
